newsitem.title: USA: Rescuers in grim search for victims of Texas twister.
newsitem.headline: Rescuers in grim search for victims of Texas twister.

text.p: Rescue teams on Wednesday picked through the battered remains of this rural Texas community in a gruesome search for victims of a powerful tornado that killed at least 27 people and left dozens homeless.
Police said the death toll could rise further as 23 people were still unaccounted for, and hopes of finding more survivors were fading fast.

"Miracles do happen in these situations but there is not much left out there. It is possible, but probably not extremely likely," said Sherri Deatherage Green, a spokeswoman with the Texas Department of Public Safety.

At least six tornadoes ripped through the heart of central Texas on Tuesday, carrying torrential rains and baseball-sized hail. In Austin, a girl drowned in a rain-swollen creek and a man was killed when his house was struck by a tornado.

But the small town of Jarrell, which sits in rolling cattle country, suffered the worst destruction with about 50 homes practically wiped off the map. Body parts, dozens of dead cattle, tattered clothes and building materials were scattered all around.

Elton Bomer, chairman of Texas' State Insurance Commission, said preliminary estimates put the damage to Jarrell at between $10 million and $20 million, and at $25 million to $50 million for the entire affected area. "That's a rough estimate. We'll know more later in the week," he said.

"I saw devastation which is hard to describe. It looked like it (the tornado) sucked the life out of the land," Gov. George W. Bush told reporters after flying over the site. He declared Williamson County a disaster area and urged federal officials to release emergency assistance as soon as possible.
Survivors said they saw the mutilated bodies of neighbours among the debris, a horse cut in two and a bull impaled on what was left of a power pole.

"One guy looked like he was nine feet tall because his body was so stretched out," local resident Billy Williams said. "I knew these people and I could barely recognise them. It was hard to take. When I saw a dead little boy, I had to leave."

Charlie Boren said he was at home sleeping after working a night shift when his wife rushed home to get him out of the tornado's path. He ran out in his underwear and they jumped into their car and raced off, escaping death by seconds.
"I was looking right down its throat when it was about to swallow me up," Boren said.

Most of those who stayed took shelter but had nowhere to hide as the tornado, packing winds of around 200 mph (320 kph), tossed homes and trucks into the air and even sucked the asphalt off the roads.
Rescue workers slogged through knee-deep mud looking for victims on Wednesday as shocked survivors waited for news of friends and families still missing in the twisted wreckage.

Jarrell, a town of about 650 people which lies 40 miles (62 km) north of Austin, was hit by a powerful tornado almost eight years ago. One person was killed then but residents said Tuesday's tornado was a force of nature they hoped never to witness again.
"This one sounded like a bear growling, low tones, an evil sound," said 17-year-old Danny Williams, who took refuge with his father when the tornado passed near their home.

In nearby Cedar Park, five people were feared killed under the collapsed roof of a grocery store which was battered by the storm, but police said on Wednesday they had searched throughout the night and were confident nobody was trapped.
In all, about 200 buildings were damaged or destroyed across a four-county area by the six twisters. About 100,000 people were temporarily without power overnight.
Meteorologists said the Jarrell twister would most likely will be categorized as an F-4 -- a devastating tornado generating winds of 207-260 miles an hour.

In human terms, the tornado is expected to rank as one of the deadliest on record in Texas. In May 1953, 114 people died when a twister devastated Waco. More recently, 42 were killed and more than 3,000 homes destroyed by an April 1979 twister that struck the city of Wichita Falls in north Texas.
